Here I created a file set that filtered for just the Big Ten teams, filtering the teams in the conference. Then we took the nunmber of total plays divided by the amount of games that the teams played in.


Code
bigten24 <- logs24 |>
  filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference")

bigten25 <- logs25 |>
  filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference")




Code
avg_plays_24 <- bigten24 |>
  group_by(Team) |>
  summarize(avg_plays = mean(TotalPlays, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(season = "2024")

avg_plays_25 <- bigten25 |>
  group_by(Team) |>
  summarize(avg_plays = mean(TotalPlays, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(season = "2025")


Sometimes, team’s offenses run a lot of plays because they want to speed up the pace of the game. But other times, it’s because their defense is unable to get any stops. Ocassionaly, it’s both. That’s what happened with 2024 Maryland, who had one of the worst passing defenses in the Big Ten, allowing opponents to throw for over 300 yards per game in a majority of its Big Ten contests. The Terps’ offense was constantly on the field and trying to play catch up, which led to them running the most amunt of plays.


Code
ggplot(avg_plays_24, aes(x = reorder(Team, avg_plays), y = avg_plays)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f77b4") +
  coord_flip() +
 labs(title = "Maryland football finished 4-8.", subtitle = "It still ran the most offensive plays in the Big Ten",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Average Offensive Plays"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









But this season, we’ve seen some drastic shifts in the conference. Ohio State, who has some of the most offensive firepower in the nation, runs the least amount of plays in the Big Ten. That’s most likely due to the Buckeyes’ blowing out several teams, but they also have had one of the nation’s best defenses, and this is a somewhat troubling sign for Ohio State’s future. One other takeaway: teams with strong and older quarterbacks tend to run more plays. Seven of the top eight teams have either old quarterbacks or a strong true freshman signal-caller in the case of Maryland and Malik Washington.


Code
ggplot(avg_plays_25, aes(x = reorder(Team, avg_plays), y = avg_plays)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#ff7f0e") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Ohio State's offense is dominant despite not running plays",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Average Offensive Plays"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Meanwhile, Maryland’s aces actually predicate alot of its scoring, compared to Nebraska.   inner_join(final_big_ten, join_by(Season))


Run the ball and prosper. When people picture Big Ten football, box scores of sub-100 passing yard days, trench warefare between offensive and defensive lines and ground-and-pound offenses pop to mind.
Jim Harbaugh’s four tight end formations, Iowa’s commitment to avoiding an efficient passing game like the plauge and the great running backs who have come through the conference (Jonathan Taylor, Kenneth Walker and Blake Corum). It’s the brand of the Big Ten: we run the ball better than anyone.
But the numbers don’t suggest that, entirely. The Big Ten actually has a number of teams who can win games without rushing the ball effectively. Compared to the NCAA average, the conference has actually become a more pass-happy league over recent years. In 2022, Big Ten teams who rushed for less than 100 yards still 9% of the conference’s total games, compared to the NCAA average of just under 6%.

  geom_line(aes(y = big_ten_low_pct_rush_wins, color = "Big Ten")) +
  labs(
    title = "Low Rush Percentage Wins: NCAA vs Big Ten",
    x = "Season", 
    y = "Low Rush Win Percentage",
    color = "Group"
  ) +

Progression is not always linear in sports. Plenty of times, you saw freshman who thrive in year struggle in their second season. Seniors who burst onto the scenes out of nowhere or juniors who completely struggle after dominating to begin their college tenures.
But in college soccer, progression seems to follow a typical trend - at least for scoring. Freshman who take the least amount of shots per game on average, followed by sophomores, then juniors and finally seniors.

##He’s known as an offenive rebounding guru, particualrly from his time at Texas A&M, when he lead the country twice. So I wanted to see if that was always the case.

buzz_orb_by_season <- buzz_teams |>
  group_by(Team, Season) |>
  summarise(
    games      = n(),
    off_reb_pg = mean(TeamOffRebounds, na.rm = TRUE),
    opp_off_pg = mean(OpponentOffRebounds, na.rm = TRUE),
